profile.campus: Google Northern Virginia (Reston / Loudoun County / Prince William County), VA
profile.address: Energy Park Drive, Sycolin, Goose Creek Village, Loudoun County, VA 20147 (2)
profile.reading:
This building is part of Google's Northern Virginia data center footprint, mapped near Leesburg along Energy Park Drive in the Sycolin/Goose Creek Village area of Loudoun County, near a neighboring Google building at Stonewall Creek Business Park. Google's own Virginia locations page, fetched this session, does not name individual buildings or addresses within its Northern Virginia footprint, so this specific structure is not independently identified beyond its OSM-derived location.

Google's cloud infrastructure operates as a business of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL/GOOG, SEC CIK 0001652044), headquartered at 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, California. Google's own Virginia data center location page, fetched fresh this session, states the company established a Virginia presence in 2009, purchased Northern Virginia land in 2017, opened its first facility in 2019, expanded a second Loudoun County facility in 2021, and opened a third in Prince William County in 2023; in 2025 Google announced a $9 billion investment for 2025-2026 spanning existing Northern Virginia sites and a new Chesterfield County campus. Google reports $15.6 billion in Virginia economic activity and over 36,000 employee volunteer hours since 2010.

Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley corridor, of which this Leesburg-area building is part, hosts large single-tenant campuses for AWS and Meta and colocation operators including Digital Realty and Equinix, all separately tracked in this registry, though Google's own public materials describe its Virginia footprint in aggregate rather than naming individual buildings or per-building capacity figures.

Loudoun and Prince William counties sit at the center of what industry trackers call Data Center Alley, the largest concentration of data center capacity in the world by aggregate power draw, a status Loudoun County's own economic development office has cited in public materials for over a decade. Dominion Energy, the regional utility, has repeatedly flagged this corridor in integrated resource plan filings with the Virginia State Corporation Commission as the single largest driver of new electricity demand in its Virginia service territory, prompting new transmission and generation investment. Virginia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption, administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership and renewed by the General Assembly, has been a material factor in Google and other hyperscalers continuing to expand in the corridor rather than building only in lower-tax states, though Google has not disclosed how much exemption value this specific facility has claimed.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley, and Google's presence there sits alongside large single-tenant campuses for AWS and Meta and colocation operators including Digital Realty and Equinix, all separately tracked in this registry. Dominion Energy is the principal electric utility serving most of the corridor and has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system. reading.body:
Google operates a data center campus in Loudoun County that spans multiple sites and is part of a larger footprint extending into Prince William County. The company announced a $1 billion expansion of these campuses in April 2024, but does not publish megawatt capacity, square footage, or exact addresses for individual buildings, only aggregate state-level investment figures.

The facility cannot be ranked within Virginia's data center capacity because no individual building-level power specification is available. Of 326 mapped facilities in the state, only 23 have published megawatt figures, totaling 1375.4 MW, and this campus does not contribute a disclosed figure to that total.

Without published capacity specifications, this campus cannot be assessed as a binding constraint on AI scaling or compared to other infrastructure investments in the region. The scale of Google's regional expansion and continued investment signals intent, but the absence of disclosed power capacity means the campus's actual role in the grid and compute landscape is not publicly knowable from operator disclosures.
